Table 3 marks no source for the value, and its smallest index, 1.1985, lies within 5 × 10⁻⁴ of nitrogen-liquid.json's 1.1981 at 670 nm and 77 K, so its rows need not all be at 94 K; its Table 2's indices are marked as the experimental values of Badoz et al. 1992, whose refractometer is accurate to 10⁻³ and who measured liquid methane at 91–106 K and its mixtures with ethane, with and without nitrogen, at 94 K and 1.5 bar (their abstract, through OpenAlex). The checks, at 670 nm: Table 2's pure-methane row, 1.2872, against methane-liquid.json's 1.2900 at 90 K carried by Lorentz–Lorenz to 94 K, 1.2869 (the WebBook's saturated liquid: 28.14191 mol/l at the triple point, 90.694 K, standing for 90 K, and 27.86634 mol/l at 94 K, https://webbook.nist.gov/cgi/fluid.cgi?Action=Data&Wide=on&ID=C74828&Type=SatP&Digits=7&THigh=95&TLow=94&TInc=1&RefState=DEF&TUnit=K&PUnit=MPa&DUnit=mol%2Fl&HUnit=kJ%2Fmol&WUnit=m%2Fs&VisUnit=uPa*s&STUnit=N%2Fm, SHA-256 f798ca4f529665d29368217893731471a9a6fe1837eec6f51348037e358bc19e, fetched 2026-10-15); its 96/0/4 C2H6/CH4/N2 row, 1.3848. Ideal mixing of molar refraction at the rows' mole fractions and measured densities (CH4's at the table's 1.2872, N2's from nitrogen-liquid.json) misses the rows by −0.0018 (96/0/4), −0.0055 (53/47/0) and −0.0042 (50/44/6) with ethane at 1.3887, and by +0.0056, −0.0010 and 0.0000 with the estimate's 1.3964; the ethane-free 0/83/17 row misses by −0.0042, so the mixtures pin the level only to about ±0.004, and the pure liquid's value is taken. Table 2's header reads "vol. per cent", but the quantities the paper's §2.2 solves for are mole fractions, Badoz et al. prepared their mixtures from each gas's volume and pressure (their abstract), and the binary row's measured 0.5686 g cm⁻³ lies nearer ideal mixing at mole fractions, 0.5660, than at volume fractions, 0.5533. The estimate ran 0.0077 high at 670 nm, as the method runs high on the measured liquids. Burton's 0.3794 cm³ g⁻¹ at 632.8 nm (University of British Columbia thesis, DOI 10.14288/1.0084897, CC BY; its abstract, through OpenAlex) holds over 1–200 amagat only: at the 96/0/4 row's 0.6530 g cm⁻³ it would give 1.410, above every measurement, where that row's own index implies 0.3587 cm³ g⁻¹, and the pure liquid's 1.3887 at the WebBook's 0.6476 g cm⁻³ implies 0.3650. Chem. 63, 263, DOI 10.1524/zpch.1969.63.5_6.263), the Lorentz–Lorenz function of liquid ethane, is closed, as is Lopez-Calvo and Manzanares 2008 (J. Phys. Chem. A 112, 1730, DOI 10.1021/jp076843v), whose abstract reports the C–H overtone Δv = 6 of liquid ethane at 100 K, past 14,000 cm⁻¹, in the red. k = 0: no open measurement of liquid ethane's visible absorption was found, and its weak C–H overtones in the red are not drawn
licence: one published index cited as a fact and a fit made here, with the gas dispersion and density (NIST Standard Reference Data) cited; no data set is copied
reduction: the fit evaluated on 380–780 nm every 5 nm, to six significant figures; k = 0. The slope is the Lorentz–Lorenz estimate's, which reaches the liquid's density from the gas's dispersion; only the level is measured
